content: Chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS) is a complex and poorly understood disorder with an uncertain cause. It is variably debilitating and affects approximately 4 out of every 1,000 adults in the United States, according to a 1999 study. The condition is also referred to by other names, such as myalgic encephalomyelitis (ME) and systemic exertion intolerance disease (SEID), the latter of which was proposed by the Institute of Medicine in 2015. For reasons that remain unclear, CFS is more commonly observed in women than in men and tends to occur most frequently in individuals in their 40s and 50s. While the condition is less prevalent among children and adolescents, studies on this demographic have produced contradictory findings regarding the extent of its occurrence. CFS is characterized by a range of symptoms, including widespread muscle pain (myalgia), joint pain (arthralgia), cognitive impairments, and chronic mental and physical exhaustion that is often severe. These symptoms typically manifest in individuals who were previously healthy and active. Despite ongoing research, there is no definitive diagnostic test or pathological finding that is universally accepted for diagnosing CFS. As a result, the diagnosis is primarily one of exclusion, relying on patient history and specific symptomatic criteria. While certain tests may assist in the diagnostic process, they are not definitive. There is broad agreement among medical professionals, researchers, and patient advocates that CFS poses a significant threat to health, well-being, and productivity. However, there is considerable controversy surrounding nearly every aspect of the disorder, including its nomenclature, diagnostic criteria, potential causes, and treatment options. Even the term chronic fatigue syndrome is contentious, as many patients feel it trivializes the severity of the illness. It is important to note that chronic fatigue syndrome is distinct from chronic fatigue, which is a common symptom in many illnesses. CFS is a multi-systemic disease and is relatively rare in comparison. Most definitions of CFS, excluding the 1991 UK Oxford criteria, require the presence of specific features. The most common of these is severe mental and physical exhaustion that is not alleviated by rest, as outlined in the 1994 Fukuda definition. Additionally, some diagnostic systems mandate that symptoms worsen with even minimal exertion. Most diagnostic criteria also require that symptoms persist for at least six months and that they cannot be attributed to other medical conditions. Patients with CFS may report a wide array of symptoms that are not included in all diagnostic criteria. These symptoms can include muscle weakness, cognitive dysfunction, hypersensitivity, orthostatic intolerance, digestive disturbances, depression, impaired immune response, and cardiac or respiratory issues. It remains unclear whether these symptoms represent co-morbid conditions or are directly caused by the underlying pathology of CFS. Some cases of CFS improve over time, and various treatments—though none are universally accepted—can provide a degree of symptom relief for many patients. However, full recovery is rare, with the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) estimating that only 5–10% of patients achieve complete resolution of symptoms.
